title: 20 Times on Top of the World! Meet the Everest Guide Who Just Won't Quit
summary: What's it like to stand on the roof of the world 20 times? Kenton Cool knows! This 52-year-old British mountain guide just broke his own record for the most Everest climbs by a non-Sherpa guide. And guess what? He's not done yet. "Maybe another two or three more times," he said after flying back to Kathmandu, Nepal. Cool reached the 8,849-meter (29,032-foot) summit on Friday. It was a busy week on Everest: on Wednesday alone, 274 climbers made it to the top—a single-day record! That's partly because a dangerous hanging ice block, called a serac, forced everyone to rush during a short window of good weather. Some guides, like record-holder Kami Rita Sherpa, think it's getting too crowded and want to limit climbers. But Cool disagrees. He says the key is making sure climbers have enough experience, not just cutting numbers. Right now, anyone with $15,000 for a permit can try, but Nepal is thinking about new rules to check skills first. Cool's advice? Climbing companies should be more careful about who they take up the mountain. After 20 summits, he's still excited—and already planning his next adventure.
why_it_matters: Even the highest mountain can be climbed with determination, but this story reminds us that nature is powerful and we must be careful and respect safety—whether on a mountain or in any big challenge you take on.

background_read: Mount Everest, at 8,849 meters, is the tallest mountain on Earth, sitting on the border between Nepal and Tibet.
Sherpas are an ethnic group from the high Himalayan valleys, famous for their ability to work at high altitudes and for guiding expeditions safely.
Kami Rita Sherpa is the overall world record holder for the most times anyone has reached the Everest summit, so Cool's record only applies to non-Sherpa guides.
Article_Structure: WHO: British mountain guide Kenton Cool and hundreds of other climbers, including Kami Rita Sherpa.
WHAT: Cool reached the summit for the 20th time—a non-Sherpa record—during a week when a single-day record of 274 climbers topped out.
WHERE: On Mount Everest in Nepal, with the story ending in Kathmandu.
WHY: To share the thrill of high-altitude climbing, but also to spark a debate about overcrowding, safety, and who should be allowed to attempt the world's highest peak.

perspectives.description: Adventurers celebrate Cool's record as inspiring, proving that with skill and grit, ordinary people can achieve extraordinary things on the world's biggest stage.
Experienced Sherpas like Kami Rita worry that too many climbers make the mountain dangerous and messy, and they want to limit numbers to protect both lives and the environment.
Some experts argue that instead of a strict limit, better training and stricter rules for climbing companies could make the mountain safer while still letting adventurous people chase their dreams.
